title: Soil geography

definition.text: The branch of physical geography that deals with how soils are distributed across the terrain.

facts.text: It studies the spatial distribution of soils in relation to topography, climate, soil life and the minerals within soils.
It sits beside geomorphology, climatology, hydrology and biogeography among the fields that study the Earth's surface.
Understanding pedogenesis explains soil distribution patterns today, the concern of soil geography, and in past geologic periods, the concern of paleopedology.
Pedodiversity was brought into pedology to analyse soil spatial patterns and soil geography and to test theories of soil formation.
The Russian Geographical Society awarded Konstantin Glinka its Lütke Gold Medal for his work on soil geography.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; mentioned on Physical geography, Natural science, Soil formation, Pedodiversity and Konstantin Glinka.

title: Tropical soils

definition.text: The soils of the humid tropics, most of them strongly leached and poor in nutrients, though some areas are fertile.

facts.text: On younger substrates, especially volcanic ones, tropical soils can be quite fertile.
Most cation exchange capacity sits on clay and humus colloids; fast leaching and decomposition in hot, wet climates remove them, explaining the apparent infertility of tropical soils.
Phosphorus is often the most deficient nutrient, because intense leaching and weathering deplete the mineral pool and, unlike nitrogen, it cannot be replenished from the air.
Leaching removes silica and leaves iron and aluminium sesquioxides, giving many tropical soils their characteristic red colour.
Unlike loess, tropical soils draw their fertility almost wholly from organic matter, whose humus holds nutrient ions and releases them to roots.
Stripped of vegetation, for example by deforestation, they can develop a surface hardpan of laterite or bauxite, a known case of irreversible degradation.
Abundant deep burrowers such as ants, termites and worms mean tropical soils often lack the argillic Bt horizons of midlatitude soils, and stonelayers often mark the base of the biomantle.
Charcoal, or biochar, is used to improve nutrient-poor tropical soils, an approach modelled on the fertile Amazonian terra preta.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; passes test 5 (used on many in-scope pages).

title: Lithosequence

definition.text: A set of soils formed under similar conditions on different parent materials, so that their profiles differ because of the parent material.

facts.text: Because the soils share similar weathering conditions, differences in composition reflect the relative weathering rates of the parent minerals.
The Goldich dissolution series, which ranks minerals by weathering rate, can be applied to lithosequences.
Studies of lithosequences give the clearest picture of the role of parent material in soil formation, including in paleosols.

notes: Phrase concept 'Climosequence, lithosequence and biosequence': only lithosequence has sentences; climosequence and biosequence have none. Mentioned on Goldich dissolution series and Paleopedology.

title: Soils of Australia

definition.text: The soils of the Australian continent, many of them extremely ancient and naturally deficient in phosphorus.

facts.text: Plants with proteoid (cluster) roots can grow in these very nutrient-poor soils, and their dense root-hair networks can absorb enough rain to prevent runoff.
The Australian Soil Classification replaced earlier systems for Australian soils, including the Factual Key (1960) and the Handbook of Australian Soils (1968).
James Arthur Prescott described them in CSIR bulletin 52, The Soils of Australia in Relation to Vegetation and Climate.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; mentioned on Cluster root, Surface runoff, Australian Soil Classification, Handbook of Australian Soils and James Arthur Prescott. Regional, but named by the syllabus.
